1 « Complures astrologi hunc (Ophiuchum seu Anguitenentem) Aesculapium
finxerunt » (Hygin.; Astr., II, 14), quia Aesculapio serpens est sacer (v. Boll,
Sphaera, p. 113). — Aegyptiorum Serapidem Graeci suo medicinae deo compara-
verunt ; cf. Preller-Jordan, Röm. Myth., t. I, p. 377.
2 Virginem caelestem « spiciferam » alii Cererem seu Matrem deorum, alii Pro-
serpinam, alii Atargatin seu Venerem esse contenderunt; cf. Bücheler, Carmina
epigraph., n° 24; Boll, Sphaera, p. 480. — Cf. supra p. 199, n. 1.
3 Cf. Ptolem. Tetrab., I, 9 : Τῶν δὲ ἐν ταῖς κεφαλαῖς (τῶν Διδύμων) δύο
λαμπρῶν ὁ μὲν ἐν τῇ προηγουμένῃ τῷ τοῦ Ἑρμοῦ, καλεῖται δὲ καὶ Ἀπόλλωνος, ὁ
δὲ ἐν τῇ ἑπομένῃ τῷ τοῦ Ἄρεως, καλεῖται δὲ Ἡρακλέους. Hermes ad Geminos
pertinere videtur quia, sicut Dioscuri (v. n. 4), gymnasiis et arti palaestricae prae-
sidet. — Quae ratio inter Telesphorum et Geminos intercedat, non perspicio. —
De Apolline, cf. n. 4.
4 « Geminos complures astrologi Castorem et Pollucem esse dixerunt ... alii
dixerunt Herculem esse et Apollinem » (Hygin, Astron., II, 22). De Hercule et
Apolline iam a priscis temporibus pro Geminis habitis, cf. supra p. 188, 10;
Sphaera. p. 124 ss., 480, n. 1.
sections.en: 1 "Many astrologers have imagined this (Ophiuchus or the Serpent-holder) to be Aesculapius" (Hygin.; Astr., II, 14), because the serpent is sacred to Aesculapius (see Boll, Sphaera, p. 113). — The Greeks compared the Serapis of the Egyptians to their own god of medicine; cf. Preller-Jordan, Röm. Myth., t. I, p. 377. 2 Some have contended that the celestial "ear-bearing" Virgin is Ceres or the Mother of the gods, others Proserpina, others Atargatis or Venus; cf. Bücheler, Carmina epigraph., n° 24; Boll, Sphaera, p. 480. — Cf. above p. 199, n. 1. 3 Cf. Ptolem. Tetrab., I, 9 : Τῶν δὲ ἐν ταῖς κεφαλαῖς (τῶν Διδύμων) δύο ('Of the two bright stars in the heads (of Gemini)') λαμπρῶν ὁ μὲν ἐν τῇ προηγουμένῃ τῷ τοῦ Ἑρμοῦ, καλεῖται δὲ καὶ Ἀπόλλωνος, ὁ ('the one in the preceding head is of Hermes, and is also called of Apollo,') δὲ ἐν τῇ ἑπομένῃ τῷ τοῦ Ἄρεως, καλεῖται δὲ Ἡρακλέους. ('and the one in the following head is of Ares, and is called of Heracles.') Hermes seems to pertain to Gemini because, just like the Dioscuri (see n. 4), he presides over gymnasia and the palaestric art. — What relationship exists between Telesphorus and Gemini, I do not perceive. — Concerning Apollo, cf. n. 4. 4 "Many astrologers have said that Gemini are Castor and Pollux ... others have said they are Hercules and Apollo" (Hygin, Astron., II, 22). Concerning Hercules and Apollo having been considered as Gemini already from ancient times, cf. above p. 188, 10; Sphaera. p. 124 ss., 480, n. 1.

summary.headline: Fixed Stars and Divine Influences
summary.text: Astrological discussion of fixed stars and their effects in nativities, especially Scorpio, Ophiuchus, Spica in Virgo, the heads of Gemini, and the bright star of the Dog. Their positions by degree, rising or setting, nocturnal or diurnal birth, and association with gods such as Asclepius, Serapis, Hermes, Telesphorus, Apollo, Heracles, and the Dioscuri determine healing, aid, apparitions, and other benefits.
